A Note Before We Begin

This book was first written as a study guide. It had the facts, the definitions, and the history. But facts on their own rarely change anybody’s mind. Stories do.

So we rewrote it.

In these pages you will meet the Hill family of Chicago’s South Side: Marcus, a young man trying to build something from a warehouse paycheck, and his grandmother Lucille, who everybody calls Mama Lou. You’ll also meet a few of the people around them. The Hills are not one real family. They are a composite, built from hundreds of conversations we have had in classrooms, church basements, barbershops, and Discord servers since Block Wall Street started teaching. If you see your own family in them, that is the point.

Everyone else you meet here, from Richard Allen to Jesse Binga to O.W. Gurley, is real, and so is every piece of history, every number, and every event we describe. Where we share Block Wall Street’s own view, we say so.

One more thing, and we mean it. This is education, not financial, legal, or tax advice. Digital assets are volatile. Every strategy in this book can lose money, and the laws and products we describe change constantly. Learn first. Start small. Verify everything. Talk to qualified professionals before you make big decisions.

Now let’s go meet Mama Lou.

Block Wall Street, Chicago

Prologue

The Coffee Can

The coffee can sat on the top shelf of Mama Lou’s pantry, behind the grits and the Argo starch, where nobody could reach it without a step stool.

Marcus found it the summer he turned eleven. He was looking for cookies. What he found instead was a red Maxwell House can with a plastic lid, stuffed so full of folded bills that the lid wouldn’t sit flat. Twenties, tens, a few hundreds rolled tight with rubber bands. He had never seen that much money in one place.

He was still standing on the step stool, holding it, when she walked in.

She didn’t yell. She took the can out of his hands, set it on the kitchen table, and sat down across from him.

“You know what this is?”

“Money,” he said.

“This is my insurance,” she said. “This is my bank. This is my burial. This is my getting-your-mama-out-of-trouble money. And I’m gonna tell you something my daddy told me. A bank is just somebody else’s coffee can. And they don’t have to give it back.”

Mama Lou was born in Mississippi in 1941. Her father sharecropped cotton on land he would never own, and every year at settlement time the landowner’s books said he owed more than he had earned. She came north to Chicago at nineteen, worked thirty-one years at a hospital laundry, raised four children, and paid two dollars a month into a burial society until the day the society folded. She owned her little brick house on the South Side, and she was proud of it. But she never trusted a bank, never bought a stock, and never once in her life borrowed money for anything.

Marcus would think about that coffee can a lot in the years ahead.

*  *  *

Here is the part Mama Lou understood better than most economists. Black Americans have never had a problem working. For four hundred years, Black labor has built this country’s farms, railroads, factories, music, and culture. Today Black Americans make up roughly 13% of the U.S. population. Yet collectively we hold only about 4% of the nation’s wealth.

That gap is not mainly about paychecks. It is about ownership.

Income comes from working. Wealth comes from owning. The families that pull ahead over generations are the ones that own things: land, businesses, stocks, buildings, patents, and now, digital assets. Those things grow while their owners sleep, and they get handed down when their owners die. Families that only earn wages have to start over every generation. When the job goes, the money goes.

For most of American history, Black families were locked out of owning the things that grow. Land was taken or never granted. Banks refused us. Neighborhoods were marked in red. Business districts were burned. So families like Mama Lou’s did what they could. They saved in coffee cans and mattresses and burial societies. They protected what little they had from institutions that had never protected them.

That instinct kept a lot of families alive. It did not make them wealthy. A coffee can doesn’t grow.

*  *  *

Years later, Marcus was twenty-four and working nights at a distribution center out by the airport when a coworker showed him a Bitcoin wallet on his phone.

“Nobody can freeze this,” the coworker said. “No bank. Nobody. It’s mine.”

Marcus thought about the coffee can.

That conversation is where this book really begins. Not with a get-rich-quick promise, because there isn’t one here, but with a question a lot of young Black people are asking right now: Is there finally a way to own things, protect them, and pass them down, without asking permission from the same institutions that shut our grandparents out?

Maybe. It depends on what we understand, and on what we build together.

To see where we are going, we first have to be honest about where the gap came from.

Chapter 1

The Ledger

In 2005, one of the largest banks in America did something unusual. It looked at its own past and told the truth.

JPMorgan Chase announced that two of its predecessor banks in Louisiana, Citizens Bank and Canal Bank, had served the plantation economy in the decades before the Civil War. Researchers the bank hired found that those two banks had accepted approximately 13,000 enslaved people as collateral on loans. When plantation owners failed to pay, the banks took possession of roughly 1,250 human beings as repayment.

Read that again slowly. Our ancestors were not only forced to work. They were the collateral. They were the thing being borrowed against.

When Mama Lou’s great-grandparents were enslaved, the law did not just deny them property. The law made them property. A planter who wanted to buy more land, build a sugar mill, or expand his operation could walk into a bank, pledge the people he claimed to own, and walk out with cash. If he couldn’t repay, the bank seized those people and sold them, the same way a bank today repossesses a car. Families were broken apart not only at auction blocks but in foreclosure proceedings.

This wasn’t a side detail of the economy. It was the engine. Historians who have studied mortgage records in Southern states have found that in places like Louisiana and South Carolina, more than eight in ten loans secured by mortgages used enslaved people as full or partial collateral. By 1860, the enslaved population was valued at roughly $3.5 billion in the money of the day, more than all the nation’s railroads and factories combined. Banks in the South bundled mortgages on land and enslaved people into bonds, and investors in New York and London bought them, collecting interest on human beings they would never see.

Think about what that means. The same financial tools this book will teach you to use, collateral, loans, bonds, leverage, were used to turn Black bodies into capital for somebody else. Our people generated enormous wealth. Not one dollar of it was ours.

We start here because it matters for everything that comes later. Later in this book, when we talk about using Bitcoin as collateral to build wealth without selling, we want you to remember who used to be the collateral. There is something worth sitting with in the idea of a great-great-grandchild of mortgaged people holding the collateral in their own hands.

*  *  *

When slavery ended, freedom came with nothing attached to it.

In January 1865, General William T. Sherman issued Special Field Order No. 15, setting aside coastal land in South Carolina, Georgia, and Florida for formerly enslaved families in plots of up to forty acres. That is where the phrase “forty acres and a mule” comes from. Thousands of families moved onto that land and started farming it.

Within months, President Andrew Johnson reversed the order and returned most of the land to the former Confederates who had owned it. The families were pushed off.

Imagine the alternative. Imagine four million people starting freedom with productive land, land that could be farmed, borrowed against, built on, and passed down. Instead, most formerly enslaved people had no land, no savings, and no way to get either. They ended up in sharecropping, working someone else’s fields for a share of the crop, buying seed and supplies on credit from the landowner’s store. At the end of every season the landowner kept the books. And somehow the books almost always said the family owed more than it earned.

That was Mama Lou’s father. He worked his entire life and died in debt on land he never owned.

*  *  *

Some families did break through. Black towns and business districts rose across the country after Reconstruction. Then, over and over again, they were destroyed.

In 1921 a white mob burned the Greenwood District of Tulsa, the community people called Black Wall Street. In 1923 the Black town of Rosewood, Florida, was attacked and wiped off the map. Those are the famous ones. There were many more, in cities and small towns whose names most people never learned. Every time a district burned, it took more than buildings. It took savings, inventory, homes, and the capital that would have financed the next generation.

We’ll come back to Greenwood later in this book, because its story has a lot to teach us.

*  *  *

Mama Lou’s house is a good example of the next chapter of the ledger.

For most American families in the twentieth century, the home was the main source of wealth. A house bought in the 1950s for a few thousand dollars might be worth hundreds of thousands today. That rise in value, called appreciation, is how millions of white families built the wealth they passed to their children.

But in the 1930s, a federal agency called the Home Owners’ Loan Corporation drew maps of American cities and color-coded neighborhoods by supposed lending risk. Neighborhoods where Black families lived were routinely shaded red and labeled hazardous. Banks and federal housing programs used those judgments to decide where loans would go. In practice, it meant Black families were denied mortgages, Black neighborhoods were starved of investment, and property values there were held down for decades. The practice became known as redlining.

Mama Lou did buy her house, eventually, but only after years of saving and at a price that left her little else. Her white coworkers at the hospital, many of whom bought in the suburbs with federally backed mortgages, watched their home values climb much faster. Same job. Same years. Very different inheritance.

*  *  *

Starting a business tells the same story. Access to capital decides who gets to build. For generations, Black entrepreneurs have been turned down for bank loans, charged more for business credit, and largely left out of investment networks. Even in recent years, Black founders have received only around one percent of venture capital funding in the United States.

And then there is inheritance, which is where the whole ledger comes together. A large share of American wealth is passed down: homes, businesses, savings, stocks. Each generation starts where the last one left off. When a family was prevented from owning anything for nearly two and a half centuries, and then blocked from land, blocked from homes, and blocked from capital for another hundred, each generation starts closer to zero.

Here is how compounding works in real life. Say a family owned a home worth $150,000 in 1980, and today it’s worth $500,000. That $350,000 increase didn’t require anyone to work harder. It just grew. Now the kids inherit it, maybe borrow against it to start a business, maybe sell it and invest. The growth keeps going.

If a family never owned the first house, the compounding never starts.

That’s the ledger. Not bad choices. Not lack of effort. A long history of being the asset instead of owning the asset, then being blocked from the assets that mattered most.

The good news is that the next chapter of the ledger hasn’t been written yet.

Chapter 2

Why We Showed Up First

Marcus’s cousin Deandra was the first person in the family to buy crypto, back in 2019. She was a graphic designer in Bronzeville, twenty-six, and she bought fifty dollars of Bitcoin on an app during her lunch break.

When she told the family at Thanksgiving, Uncle Ray laughed so hard he had to put his fork down.

“Internet money,” he said. “Girl, you might as well buy a lottery ticket.”

Ray had his reasons for being skeptical. But the joke landed differently than he expected, because Deandra wasn’t unusual. Across the country, Black Americans were getting into crypto in large numbers, often faster than white investors. One widely cited 2022 survey of American investors found that roughly a quarter of Black Americans owned cryptocurrency, compared with about 15% of white Americans.

That didn’t happen by accident. There were reasons, and most of them trace back to the ledger.

*  *  *

The first reason is simple. Crypto didn’t ask for permission.

When Mama Lou was young, investing in the stock market meant knowing someone. You needed a bank account, a broker, a minimum deposit, and a certain comfort level walking into offices downtown where nobody looked like you. Credit history mattered. Connections mattered. Every step had a gatekeeper, and gatekeepers had a long habit of keeping the gate shut.

Deandra didn’t need any of that. She needed a phone, an internet connection, and a digital wallet. She could buy five dollars’ worth of Bitcoin if she wanted to. Nobody could turn her down because of her zip code.

*  *  *

The second reason is trust, or rather the lack of it.

Uncle Ray lost his house in 2009.

He had been a city bus mechanic for eighteen years. In 2005 a mortgage broker came to his church and talked him into refinancing his home into a loan with a low starting payment. Ray didn’t understand that the rate would reset. When it did, his payment jumped by hundreds of dollars a month. When the housing market collapsed, the house was worth less than he owed. He was one of millions.

Ray’s story was not rare in Black neighborhoods. During the years before the 2008 crisis, Black borrowers were steered into subprime loans at much higher rates than white borrowers with similar credit, and several major lenders later paid large settlements over allegations of exactly that. Add payday lenders on every other corner, rent-to-own stores, and high-interest car loans, and a lot of Black families learned the same lesson Mama Lou learned: the financial system is not neutral, and it is often not on your side.

Then, in 2008, the country watched giant banks that had caused the crisis get rescued with public money while ordinary families lost their homes.

Bitcoin was launched in January 2009, in the wreckage of that crisis. Its anonymous creator even embedded a newspaper headline about bank bailouts in the very first block. For people like Deandra, a financial system with no bank in the middle was not an abstract idea. It was an answer to something they had lived through.

*  *  *

The third reason is how information travels in our communities.

When institutions don’t serve you, you learn to rely on each other. That’s been true since the mutual aid societies of the 1700s, and it’s still true. Deandra didn’t learn about Bitcoin from a financial advisor. She learned from a friend’s Instagram, then a YouTube channel, then a Twitter Spaces conversation, then a class in a church basement. Knowledge moved person to person, the way news about jobs and apartments always has.

That network is powerful. It can also spread bad information and scams just as fast, which is why real education matters so much.

*  *  *

The last few reasons have to do with who we are right now. The Black population in the United States is younger on average than the country as a whole, and younger people adopt new technology first. Crypto lets you buy tiny fractions of an asset, so you can start with whatever you have. And there’s a deep hunger in our community for something that crypto people call sovereignty: the ability to hold your money yourself, without anyone being able to freeze it, close your account, or decide you don’t qualify.

In Mama Lou’s terms, it was a coffee can nobody else could open. But unlike her coffee can, it could grow.

Uncle Ray wasn’t convinced. Not yet. But he stopped laughing.

Chapter 3

The Year Everything Stopped

In March 2020, the distribution center where Marcus worked didn’t shut down. It got busier. Everybody was ordering everything online, and the trucks never stopped.

But his mother, who did hair out of a salon on 79th Street, lost her income overnight. His friend Tasha, who had just signed a lease on her own nail shop, watched it sit dark for months. His cousin Jaylen got laid off from a hotel downtown with a two-week paycheck and a handshake.

For a lot of young people, 2020 was the year the old promises broke.

The formula most of us were raised on went like this: work hard, get a stable job, save money, retire comfortably. The pandemic showed how thin that was. Jobs that felt permanent disappeared in a week. Whole industries closed. People who had done everything right found out that one paycheck is one layoff away from zero, and that most families, especially Black families, didn’t have the savings to wait it out.

A lot of young people came out of that year asking a different question. Not “How do I get a good job?” but “How do I build income that doesn’t depend on one job?”

*  *  *

The internet had already been quietly answering that question. By 2020 you could run a business from a laptop. People were freelancing, selling products online, building audiences, doing content, consulting across time zones. Money had already moved into screens and apps for this generation. Paying with a phone felt normal. So when crypto showed up, a market open twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, reachable from the same phone, it didn’t feel strange. It felt like the next app.

Marcus opened his first account that year. He bought a hundred dollars of Bitcoin with his stimulus money. He also, like a lot of people that year, bought some coins he’d heard about on social media that went to almost nothing within six months.

“That second part,” he’d say later, “was my tuition.”

*  *  *

Social media was a double-edged sword in all of this. It spread financial education faster than any school ever had. People who had never been taught about compound interest, credit, or investing were suddenly learning from creators who looked like them and talked like them. At the same time, it spread hype, pump-and-dump schemes, and people selling courses on how to get rich from people who got rich selling courses.

The ones who lasted were the ones who figured out the difference between a trade and an investment, between noise and knowledge.

*  *  *

Under all of it was something deeper. This generation watched their parents live through the 2008 crash. Some watched grandparents talk about the Depression. Now they had lived through their own economic shock before thirty. The lesson they took from it was about ownership. Renting your time to someone else wasn’t enough. You needed assets, things that grow and pay you whether or not you clock in.

Crypto wasn’t the only answer to that question. But for millions of young people, it was the first door that opened.

Chapter 4

Same Percentage, Different Life

Marcus had a good year in 2021. The hundred dollars of Bitcoin he’d bought with his stimulus money grew to about nine hundred at the peak. He was proud of that, and he should have been. He multiplied his money nine times.

Around the same time, he read about an investor who had put ten million dollars into Bitcoin at the same time and rode the same run.

Same asset. Same timing. Same percentage. Marcus made eight hundred dollars. The investor made eighty million.

That’s the capital gap in one sentence.

*  *  *

More Black Americans are investing than ever before. That’s real progress. But participation isn’t the same as power. When two people both earn a 10x return, the one who started with $1,000 ends up with $10,000, and the one who started with $1,000,000 ends up with $10,000,000. Both of them made the smart move. Only one of them changed their family’s future.

This is why wealth gaps can grow even when opportunity looks equal. Returns multiply whatever you bring to the table. When you bring less because of everything in Chapter 1, even the same good decision produces a smaller result.

*  *  *

Starting capital also buys you time and patience. An investor with plenty of money can hold through a crash because they don’t need to sell to pay rent. A young person investing their last few hundred dollars often has to sell at the worst possible moment when their car breaks down.

Early investors in any new technology tend to benefit the most, because they get in before prices reflect the future. But being early only helps if you’re early with enough to matter, and if you can afford to wait.

*  *  *

When a whole community is short on capital, the problem gets bigger than any one family. Local businesses can’t get funded. Buildings are owned by people who don’t live there. Profits made in the neighborhood leave the neighborhood. Decisions about the block get made by outside investors who will never walk down it.

So what do communities do when individuals don’t have enough?

They pool.

It’s the oldest move in our playbook. Mutual aid societies, church building funds, investment clubs, credit unions, rotating savings circles that go by different names in different cultures. When ten people put in a thousand dollars each, they have ten thousand dollars together, and ten thousand dollars can do things a thousand dollars can’t.

What’s new is that the digital age has given us better tools for pooling than we’ve ever had. You’ll see how in the chapters ahead.

“So I’m not supposed to feel good about my eight hundred dollars?” Marcus asked when he first heard all this.

You should. Eight hundred dollars is real money, and it’s a start. But a start is exactly what it is. The real question is how to get from starting to building.

Chapter 5

A Bank With No Building

Uncle Ray finally asked the question at a cookout in 2022.

“So explain it to me. Where’s the bank?”

Deandra tried. “There isn’t one.”

“Then who’s lending the money?”

“Other people. And code.”

Ray shook his head. But he kept listening.

*  *  *

Start with how a regular bank works, because most of us never really think about it. You deposit money. The bank pays you maybe one percent interest on your savings, sometimes less. Then the bank lends your money to other people at six, ten, fifteen percent or more on loans and credit cards. The difference between what it pays you and what it charges them is the bank’s profit. Along the way, the bank decides who gets approved, who gets a good rate, and who gets turned away.

The bank is the middleman. It holds everyone’s money, sets the rules, and keeps the spread.

Decentralized finance, or DeFi, asks a simple question: What if the middleman were software?

*  *  *

The heart of DeFi is something called a smart contract. It’s just a computer program that lives on a blockchain and runs automatically when certain conditions are met. A simple one might say: if a borrower deposits enough collateral, release the loan. If the collateral drops too low, sell it to repay the lender. Nobody has to approve it. Nobody can look at your name or your zip code and decide you don’t qualify. The rules are written in code, and the code runs the same for everybody.

With smart contracts, people have rebuilt many of the services a bank provides. There are lending platforms where you can deposit crypto and earn interest from borrowers. There are borrowing platforms where you can put up crypto as collateral and take a loan against it. There are decentralized exchanges where you can trade one asset for another directly from your own wallet, without handing your money to a company. And more and more of it can be automated.

Because everything happens on a public blockchain, anyone can look at how much money is in a lending pool, what rates are being paid, and how loans are performing. Compare that with a traditional bank, where most of what happens behind the counter is private.

And because the code doesn’t care who you are, DeFi is open to anyone with a phone and an internet connection, anywhere on earth.

*  *  *

None of this means DeFi is safe. It isn’t, at least not automatically. Code can have bugs, and hackers look for them constantly. Prices can crash fast, and when they do, collateral gets sold automatically whether you’re watching or not. Rules and regulations are still being written. And there is no customer service line. If you send money to the wrong address, it’s gone.

Ray listened to all of that, then said the most important thing anyone said that afternoon.

“So it’s a bank that can’t discriminate against me. But it also can’t save me from myself.”

That’s exactly right. DeFi takes away the gatekeeper. It also takes away the safety net. That trade-off is the whole game, and learning to play it well is what the rest of this book is about.

Chapter 6

The Record Nobody Can Erase

When Mama Lou’s father died in 1968, the landowner’s books said he still owed $212.

Nobody in the family ever saw those books. Nobody could check the math. The only record of forty years of labor was a ledger kept by the man who profited from it, and his word was final.

Marcus thought about that the first time someone explained to him what a blockchain actually is.

*  *  *

A blockchain is a record book. That’s all. It records transactions: who sent what to whom, and when. What makes it different is who keeps it.

In the old world, one party holds the ledger. The bank keeps the record of your account. The county keeps the record of your deed. The landowner keeps the record of what the sharecropper owes. If the keeper makes a mistake, or lies, or loses the book in a fire, you’re at their mercy.

A blockchain flips that. Instead of one keeper, thousands of computers around the world, called nodes, each hold a complete copy of the record. When new transactions happen, they’re grouped into a block. The network checks that each transaction is valid, that nobody is spending money they don’t have, and then the block is added to the chain, linked to every block before it.

Once a block is on the chain, changing it would mean rewriting every block after it on thousands of computers at the same time, while everyone else is watching. In a network as large as Bitcoin’s, that’s practically impossible. The record becomes permanent.

*  *  *

It’s also public. On most blockchains, anyone can look up any transaction ever made. You don’t need permission. You don’t need to trust the bookkeeper, because there isn’t one. You can check the math yourself.

Cryptography holds it all together. Each person controls their funds with a private key, a secret code that only they know, which proves ownership without revealing the key itself. Nobody else can move your money without it.

And there’s no central authority. No single company, government, or person can shut the Bitcoin network down, reverse your transaction, or freeze your account. That makes it harder to censor and harder to manipulate. It also means there’s no one to call if something goes wrong.

*  *  *

People like to compare blockchain to roads or the internet, and it’s a fair comparison. Roads made commerce possible. The internet made instant communication possible. Blockchain makes it possible to move and record value without trusting a middleman. It’s infrastructure. Other things get built on top of it.

For communities that have spent generations at the mercy of somebody else’s ledger, that matters. A permanent, public record that anyone can verify is not a small thing. It’s the opposite of the landowner’s book.

“If they’d had this back then,” Mama Lou said, when Marcus explained it to her at her kitchen table, “my daddy could have checked the numbers.”

“Yes, ma’am.”

She was quiet for a while. “Well,” she said. “Y’all check the numbers now.”

Chapter 7

Beyond the Coins

Deandra had been designing album covers and flyers for Chicago artists for six years. She loved the work. She hated the math.

A cover she designed for $400 could end up on merchandise, posters, and streaming platforms seen by millions of people. Somebody made real money from it. It wasn’t her. Once she sold the file, it was gone. The internet copied it a thousand times, and she never saw another dollar.

That was the problem with the internet for creators. Everything could be copied. Nothing could be owned.

*  *  *

Most people think crypto means coins. Bitcoin, Ethereum, whatever’s trending that week. But the coins are only one piece. The bigger idea is that blockchains can prove who owns what, including things that were never ownable before.

That’s where NFTs came in. The letters stand for non-fungible token. “Fungible” means interchangeable: one dollar bill is the same as any other dollar bill. A non-fungible token is one of a kind. It’s a unique digital record on a blockchain that proves ownership of a specific item, whether that’s a piece of digital art, a song, a ticket, a membership, or even the title to something physical.

The 2021 NFT boom was full of hype and speculation, and a lot of people lost money. Deandra watched most of the projects she followed collapse. But under the noise was something real, and she saw it.

With an NFT, a creator can build royalties into the token itself. Every time the piece resells, a percentage can automatically flow back to the original artist. Think about what that would have meant for the Black musicians of the twentieth century, many of whom signed away their masters for a flat fee and watched labels collect on their work for the rest of their lives. Royalty enforcement varies by marketplace today, and it isn’t guaranteed. But the idea that ownership and payment can follow the work, forever, through code, is a big one.

Deandra’s point was simple. “Our culture drives what the whole world listens to, wears, and says. We’ve never owned it. This is the first tool I’ve seen that could change that.”

*  *  *

The other big idea beyond the coins is fractional ownership.

A building on the South Side might cost two million dollars. Almost nobody in the neighborhood can buy it alone. So it gets bought by an investor from somewhere else, and the rent checks leave the neighborhood every month.

But what if that building were divided into two million digital shares, each worth a dollar? Suddenly a teacher, a nurse, and a warehouse worker could each own a piece, and each collect a share of the rent. That’s what tokenization makes possible: dividing high-value assets like real estate, art, or businesses into small pieces anyone can buy.

We’ll come back to tokenization in a big way in Chapter 18, because since the first edition of this book, it has moved from an idea to one of the fastest-growing corners of finance.

These tools are still young. They carry real risks, and a lot of projects fail. But they point toward a world where the people who create value can own a piece of it. For a community that has created so much and owned so little, that’s worth paying attention to.

Chapter 8

Renters of the Internet

Marcus drove for a rideshare app on weekends in 2022 to make extra money. One Sunday night, sitting in his car outside a club in River North waiting for a ping, he did the math.

He was providing the car. He was paying for the gas, the insurance, the maintenance, and the phone. He was providing the labor and the late nights. The app took a cut of every ride, and it hadn’t built a single car.

And the app’s early investors? They had become rich.

That night Marcus understood the difference between a consumer and an owner.

*  *  *

Most of us live in a consumer economy. We spend money on platforms, apps, and services that belong to somebody else. We scroll the feeds, fill the carts, stream the songs, and drive the cars. Every tap makes money for the owners. When millions of people use a platform, the owners capture enormous value through transaction fees, advertising, and subscriptions.

The people who created the most wealth in the internet era weren’t the heaviest users. They were the people who built the infrastructure, and the people who owned pieces of it early. The distance between using technology and owning technology became one of the biggest wealth gaps of the last thirty years.

Black Americans have been some of the most influential users of the internet. We shape culture online. We create trends that billion-dollar companies profit from. But we have owned very little of the platforms where that culture lives. In the internet era, we were renters.

*  *  *

Blockchains offer a chance at a different arrangement.

Many blockchain networks issue tokens that give holders a stake in the network itself: a vote in how it’s governed, a share of fees, or both. This is sometimes called protocol ownership. Instead of a company owned by a handful of founders and investors, a network can be owned, at least in part, by the people who use it and build it. Entrepreneurs can build open networks instead of traditional companies, and the value can be spread more widely.

None of that is automatic. Plenty of tokens are worthless, and plenty of “community-owned” projects are really controlled by insiders. But the possibility is real, and it’s new.

*  *  *

The biggest shift here isn’t technical. It’s mental.

The consumer question is: “How can I use this technology?”

The owner’s question is: “How can I build something on top of this technology, or own a piece of what’s being built?”

That second question is where wealth comes from. It’s what the builders of the railroads, the factories, and the internet all asked. And for the first time, the infrastructure being built is open. You don’t need permission to build on it.

Marcus still drives on weekends sometimes. But now, when he sits outside a club waiting for a ping, he’s usually reading about how the thing he’s using actually works.

Back to contents

Chapter 9

Learning to Build

Jaylen, the cousin who got laid off from the downtown hotel in 2020, spent the next year teaching himself to code.

He started with free videos on YouTube at his mother’s kitchen table. Then free online courses. Then a cheap bootcamp. He failed at a lot of it. Some nights he stared at an error message for two hours before realizing he’d forgotten a comma.

By 2023 he was working remotely as a junior developer for a company in Atlanta, making more than twice what the hotel paid him. By 2025 he was writing smart contracts.

“The hotel paid me to carry other people’s bags,” he said. “Now I get paid to build the thing.”

*  *  *

Every era has had its infrastructure. Railroads, then oil, then electricity, then telecommunications, then the internet. In each era, the biggest fortunes went to the people who built and controlled the systems everyone else depended on.

Today the infrastructure is digital. The most valuable companies in the world don’t make physical things. They make the software and networks that commerce, communication, and increasingly money run on. And the skills that build those systems have become some of the most valuable skills a person can have.

Several areas matter especially in the blockchain economy. Software development is the foundation of everything. Blockchain engineering builds and maintains the networks themselves. Smart contract development writes the code that runs DeFi, and because a bug in a smart contract can cost millions, people who write that code well are in high demand. Cybersecurity protects digital systems from theft, and in a world where money is code, security is everything. Digital product design makes these tools usable for regular people, which may be the biggest challenge in the whole industry.

*  *  *

The most powerful thing about this moment is that the education is out there. A lot of it is free. It doesn’t require being admitted to anything. Jaylen didn’t need a college degree in computer science. He needed a laptop, an internet connection, and a stubborn streak.

That doesn’t mean it’s easy. It’s hard, and it takes time. But the door isn’t locked the way so many doors were for Mama Lou’s generation.

The goal isn’t for everyone to become a programmer. The goal is for enough of us to become builders that the next generation of financial infrastructure isn’t built entirely by other people, for other people.

Back to contents

Chapter 10

When the Code Is the Contract

Tasha finally opened her nail shop again in 2022. She was careful this time. She read every word of the lease. She got a lawyer to look at it. She’d learned from 2020 what a bad contract can do to you.

So when Marcus started talking to her about smart contracts, she asked the right question.

“Who enforces it?”

“The code does.”

“And if the code is wrong?”

Marcus didn’t have a good answer. That’s the right place to start this chapter.

*  *  *

Technology might power the digital economy, but law decides who owns what, who owes what, and what happens when something goes wrong. A contract, in the traditional sense, is an agreement enforced by courts. If one side doesn’t hold up their end, the other side can sue.

A smart contract is different. It’s an agreement written as code that carries itself out automatically. A simple one might say: if a buyer sends payment, transfer ownership of the digital asset. No court, no lawyer, no waiting. The code runs the moment the condition is met.

People in crypto sometimes say “code is law.” What they mean is that the rules written into the software are the rules, full stop. The system executes agreements continuously, around the clock, without needing anyone to trust anyone.

That’s powerful. Smart contracts can split payments automatically among a band, a producer, and a songwriter every time a song earns money. They can distribute profits to every member of an investment group the instant revenue arrives. They can lay out voting rules for a community fund so that nobody can move money without approval. They can protect digital property and intellectual property by recording ownership permanently.

*  *  *

But Tasha’s question matters. Code can be wrong. It can be written badly, or it can be exploited by someone who spots a flaw. When that happens, “code is law” can mean your money is gone and the code says that’s fine.

And the real world still has real laws. Owning a token doesn’t automatically give you legal rights, and a smart contract doesn’t override tax law, securities law, or consumer protection law. Courts and regulators are still working out how all of this fits together.

That’s why legal knowledge is becoming as valuable as technical knowledge. The people who will do best in this new economy understand both: how the code works, and how the law treats it.

Tasha still reads every contract. Now she reads the code, too, or at least she makes sure somebody she trusts has.

Back to contents

Chapter 11

Pooling

Mama Lou’s burial society met on the second Sunday of every month in the basement of a church on Indiana Avenue.

Everybody paid their two dollars. Sister Maxine kept the book. When a member died, the society paid for the funeral, the casket, and the repast, so no family had to beg or go into debt to bury their mother. Two dollars a month from forty people meant nobody faced the worst day of their life alone.

It worked for decades. Then, in the 1980s, Sister Maxine got sick, nobody else knew how to keep the book, some members stopped paying, and one year the money just wasn’t there when it was needed. The society quietly folded. Mama Lou never got back what she’d put in.

There are two lessons in that story. The first is that pooling works. The second is that pooling needs good systems, or it breaks when the person holding it together is gone.

*  *  *

The first lesson runs through all of Black history. Communities that organize economically build more power than individuals acting alone. Mutual aid societies, church funds, cooperatives, credit unions, investment clubs, neighborhood business alliances. By pooling resources, communities build things no single person could.

The second lesson is where new technology comes in.

*  *  *

A DAO, which stands for decentralized autonomous organization, is a kind of digital organization that runs on a blockchain. Members pool money into a shared treasury. The rules for how that money can be spent are written into smart contracts. Members vote on decisions, often using tokens that represent their share. And every transaction is recorded publicly, so every member can see exactly where the money is and where it went.

Think about Mama Lou’s burial society with those tools. The book keeps itself. Every member can check the balance on their phone. Nobody can quietly take money out, because the rules require a vote. And when Sister Maxine gets sick, the system doesn’t depend on her.

DAOs aren’t perfect. Voting can be dominated by a few big holders. Smart contracts can have bugs. Many DAOs have no clear legal status, which can create real problems for members. But the idea of community ownership of shared money, with transparent rules that don’t depend on one person’s honesty or one person’s health, is exactly what our grandparents’ institutions needed and didn’t have.

In Chapter 19, we’ll look at how communities can actually set up shared funds today, with more tools than DAOs alone.

Back to contents

Chapter 12

The Long Way Home

Deandra went to Ghana in 2019 for what the government there called the Year of Return, marking four hundred years since the first enslaved Africans arrived in the English colony of Virginia. She stood in the door of Cape Coast Castle, the door the enslaved walked through onto the ships, and she cried in a way she couldn’t explain for weeks afterward.

She also made a friend, Kofi, a young software developer in Accra.

A year later, Kofi needed help paying for a certification course. Deandra wanted to send him two hundred dollars. The wire transfer fee and exchange rate were going to eat a real chunk of it, and it would take days. So she sent him USDC, a digital dollar, from her phone. It arrived in about a minute, for a few cents.

That was the day she understood what people mean when they say blockchains don’t have borders.

*  *  *

Traditional finance is built around nations. Banks operate within countries. Currencies are controlled by governments. Moving money across borders means passing through a chain of banks, each taking a fee and adding delay. For families sending money home, those fees add up to billions of dollars a year.

Blockchain networks live on the internet, and the internet is global. A wallet in Chicago and a wallet in Accra are equally close.

*  *  *

The African diaspora is one of the largest and most widely spread communities on earth. Across the United States, the Caribbean, Latin America, Europe, and the African continent itself, hundreds of millions of people share roots, and in many cases share economic interests they’ve never been able to act on together.

Blockchain creates new possibilities for that global family. Faster and cheaper remittances. Investment that can flow directly from the diaspora into African businesses, and back. Shared funds and cooperatives with members on multiple continents. Access to financial tools for the many Africans who have phones but no bank account.

It’s not all simple. Every country has its own laws. Scams follow money everywhere. And technology alone doesn’t create trust between people who have never met. But for the first time, the infrastructure for a truly global Black economy exists.

Kofi finished his certification. Today he and Deandra are working on a small project together, a Chicago designer and an Accra developer, building something neither of them could have built alone. The long way home, it turns out, can go both directions.

Back to contents

Chapter 13

We’ve Seen This Movie Before

When Uncle Ray was a boy in the 1960s, his grandfather used to tell him about the first time he saw an electric light in a house.

“People said it was dangerous,” his grandfather said. “They said it would burn the house down. Some houses did burn down. Then everybody had it.”

Ray told that story at a family dinner in 2024, and Deandra laughed out loud, because it was almost word for word what he’d said about Bitcoin five years earlier.

*  *  *

Major technologies tend to follow a pattern. First comes invention, and hardly anyone notices. Then comes a wave of excitement and speculation, with money pouring in and wild promises everywhere. Then comes a crash, when a lot of people lose money and everyone declares the whole thing a fraud. Then, quietly, the real building happens. Years later, the technology is so normal nobody thinks about it.

Railroads went through this in the 1800s, with speculative manias and brutal crashes. Electricity did too. So did the automobile, the radio, and the telephone. The internet had its dot-com bubble, when companies with no profits were worth billions, and then the crash of 2000 and 2001, when most of them disappeared. People said the internet had been overhyped.

Twenty-five years later, the internet runs the world. Some of the companies that survived the crash are now among the most valuable companies in history.

*  *  *

Blockchain looks like it’s moving through a similar cycle. It has had its manias and its crashes, its frauds and its failures. The collapse of several major crypto companies in 2022 wiped out billions of dollars and many people’s savings. Yet in the years since, big financial institutions have moved in, not out: spot Bitcoin ETFs, tokenized stocks and funds, stablecoin laws, and even mortgages backed by Bitcoin. You’ll read about several of those in the chapters ahead.

Understanding the pattern doesn’t tell anyone what happens next. Nobody can predict that. But it helps you stay steady. When prices crash, people panic. People who understand technological history know that crashes are often part of how new technology matures. They also know that not every project survives, which is why curiosity has to be paired with critical thinking.

“So I was wrong,” Ray said, finally, at that dinner.

“You were early,” Deandra said. “Just in the wrong direction.”

Everybody laughed. Then Ray asked her to show him how to set up a wallet.

Back to contents

Chapter 14

The Institutions We Built Before

Mama Lou’s burial society wasn’t the first of its kind. It was one of the last of a long line that stretches back more than two hundred years.

In 1787, in Philadelphia, two free Black men named Richard Allen and Absalom Jones founded the Free African Society. Members paid small dues into a shared fund, and the fund took care of the sick, the widowed, and the orphaned. No bank would insure a Black family in those days. So Black families insured each other.

Over the next century, that idea spread everywhere Black people lived. Benevolent societies. Burial associations. Fraternal orders. Church relief funds. Most of them ran on the same simple principle: many small contributions add up to something strong enough to handle what no single family could handle alone.

Every community wealth strategy in this book grows from that root.

*  *  *

After the Civil War, Congress chartered a bank specifically for the newly freed. The Freedman’s Savings and Trust Company opened in 1865, and Black families trusted it with everything they had. Soldiers deposited their pay. Washerwomen deposited their coins. Churches deposited their building funds. Within a few years the bank held millions of dollars.

But the people running the bank were not the people who owned the deposits. The bank was badly managed. Money was moved into risky loans and speculation. In 1874 it collapsed. Tens of thousands of depositors lost their savings, and many recovered only a fraction, years later, if at all.

That failure echoed for generations. It’s part of why Mama Lou’s father didn’t trust banks, and why she kept a coffee can. The lesson was harsh, and it’s still true: when you don’t control the institution holding your money, your money is only as safe as the people who do.

*  *  *

Then there’s Greenwood.

In the early 1900s, in Tulsa, Oklahoma, a Black businessman named O.W. Gurley bought land north of the railroad tracks and sold it only to Black buyers. J.B. Stradford built a hotel there that was among the finest Black-owned hotels in the country. Around them grew a district of grocery stores and restaurants, doctors’ and lawyers’ offices, theaters, churches, schools, and newspapers. Segregation kept Black residents out of white businesses, so the money earned in Greenwood tended to stay in Greenwood, passing from hand to hand before it ever left. People called it Black Wall Street.

On May 31 and June 1, 1921, a white mob attacked. Roughly thirty-five city blocks were burned to the ground. Estimates of the dead run into the hundreds. Thousands of people were left homeless overnight. Insurance claims were largely denied.

Greenwood’s wealth was real. But it was stored in things that could be burned: buildings, inventory, cash in the till. It could be destroyed in a night, and it was.

*  *  *

Closer to home, Chicago built its own Black metropolis.

During the Great Migration, hundreds of thousands of Black Southerners came north, many of them to the South Side, to the neighborhood that came to be called Bronzeville. They built a city within a city.

A man named Jesse Binga opened a private bank there in 1908. It became the Binga State Bank, one of the first Black-owned banks in Chicago. Black insurance companies grew up nearby, including the firms that later came together as Supreme Liberty Life Insurance, offering coverage to families that white insurers wouldn’t touch.

Bronzeville also ran on another, unofficial financial system: the policy game. It was a numbers lottery, played every day on nearly every block. It was illegal, and it took a lot of money from a lot of poor people. We don’t hold it up as a model. But historians have documented how some of the men who ran it, the “policy kings,” used their profits to bankroll legitimate Black businesses, lend to entrepreneurs the banks ignored, and fund community institutions. In a city where formal capital was closed to Black Chicagoans, the policy game worked as a rough, parallel capital market.

When the Great Depression hit, the Binga State Bank failed in 1930, and other Black banks followed. Depositors had few protections and few other places to turn. Once again, a community’s savings disappeared.

*  *  *

Put these stories side by side and a pattern jumps out. Black communities could build. They did build, again and again, even under terrible conditions. But their wealth kept getting stored in forms that could be burned, seized, or frozen, in institutions they didn’t control or that the law left unprotected, in places where local hostility could reach it.

That is exactly where the digital tools in this book become more than a curiosity.

Bitcoin doesn’t fix racism, bad policy, or bad decisions. But it changes some of the conditions that made Black wealth so easy to destroy. It can be held in self-custody, without depending on any bank. It can be carried across cities and borders in the form of a recovery phrase. Its records are transparent, so members of a shared fund can verify balances themselves. Its rules can be written into code and multi-signature wallets, so no single person can walk off with the money. And anyone with a phone can take part.

A building on Greenwood Avenue could be burned. A well-secured Bitcoin reserve, split across several keyholders in different places, is a lot harder to destroy.

*  *  *

That’s why Block Wall Street’s long-term work is aimed at rebuilding the institutions Greenwood and Bronzeville once had, on a stronger foundation. The programs we are designing to build ourselves include a community treasury to pool and deploy capital into community projects, a Bitcoin-backed mortgage program to help members turn digital assets into homeownership, a health fund and mutual aid society that picks up where the benevolent societies left off, and a mining and agriculture site that pairs Bitcoin mining with food and land.

Every one of those is an old idea. The burial society. The Binga Bank. The insurance company. The family farm. What’s new is what we’re building them on.

Even the policy game has a lawful modern cousin. There are now “no-loss” prize savings systems where people pool their deposits, the pool earns interest, and the interest is paid out as prizes, while every participant keeps their original deposit. All the excitement of hitting the number. None of the losing.

Chapter 15

The Collateral

In June 2026, Marcus called his grandmother with news.

“Mama Lou, you remember that Bitcoin I’ve been buying?”

“The internet money.”

“Somebody in Michigan just bought a house with it. And they didn’t sell any of it.”

She was quiet for a second. “How you buy a house with something you didn’t sell?”

That’s the question this whole chapter answers.

*  *  *

Most people think about an investment in two steps: buy it, and someday sell it. Wealthy families think about it in three. The third step is to borrow against it.

Rich families with big stock portfolios or valuable real estate rarely sell their best assets to pay for their lives. When they need money, they borrow against those assets. They keep ownership. The assets keep growing. And in the United States, taking out a loan generally isn’t a taxable event the way selling is.

Selling has costs most people don’t think about. You may owe capital gains tax on the profit. You lose all of the asset’s future growth. And people who sell often end up buying back later at a higher price, or never getting back in at all. Plenty of early Bitcoin holders sold coins to pay for a car or a bill and watched those coins become worth many times more.

Collateral is what makes the third step possible. Collateral is simply an asset you pledge to secure a loan. If you don’t repay, the lender takes it.

At Block Wall Street, we sum up this idea in three words: Don’t sell. Collateralize.

*  *  *

Before we go any further, we have to go back to Chapter 1.

For generations, our ancestors were the collateral. Planters walked into banks, pledged the human beings they claimed to own, and walked out with loans. Those loans built plantations, sugar mills, and fortunes. When planters defaulted, the banks took the people. The same financial tools you are about to learn, collateral, loan-to-value, liquidation, were used to turn Black bodies into somebody else’s credit line.

We don’t bring this up to shock anyone. We bring it up because it changes how this chapter should feel. When the descendants of mortgaged people learn to hold the collateral themselves, to borrow against assets they own instead of being the asset someone else borrows against, that isn’t just a financial strategy. It’s a reversal.

Hold that thought. Now let’s talk about how it actually works, because it can hurt you if you don’t understand it.

*  *  *

Every collateralized loan has a number called loan-to-value, or LTV. It’s just the loan divided by the value of the collateral.

Say Marcus deposits $10,000 worth of Bitcoin and borrows $3,000. His LTV is $3,000 divided by $10,000, which is 30%.

Every lender also sets a liquidation threshold. If the price of Bitcoin falls far enough that the LTV climbs past that threshold, the lender automatically sells some or all of the collateral to pay off the loan. For Bitcoin on major lending platforms, thresholds somewhere between 70% and 80% are common, though every platform is different.

Let’s use 78%. Marcus owes $3,000. His collateral would have to fall to about $3,846 before liquidation kicks in, because $3,000 divided by 0.78 is $3,846. That means Bitcoin would have to drop roughly 62% from where he borrowed.

Now imagine Marcus had gotten greedy and borrowed $7,000 against that same $10,000. That’s a 70% LTV. A drop of only about 10% would put him at the edge.

Bitcoin has fallen by more than half several times in its history. It will likely happen again. The difference between the Marcus who borrowed $3,000 and the Marcus who borrowed $7,000 is the difference between riding out a crash and being wiped out by one.

Low LTV isn’t timid. It’s how you survive.

*  *  *

For years, Bitcoin-backed loans lived almost entirely on crypto platforms. Then the traditional system started moving.

In June 2025, the Federal Housing Finance Agency directed Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, the giant government-sponsored companies at the center of the American mortgage market, to prepare to consider crypto holdings when evaluating mortgages. On March 26, 2026, mortgage lender Better Home & Finance and Coinbase announced a Fannie Mae-eligible mortgage that lets buyers pledge Bitcoin or the USDC stablecoin toward a down payment instead of selling. In June 2026, they announced the first one had been funded, for a couple in Michigan, with plans to roll it out nationwide.

Here’s how the companies described it. The buyer takes out a normal Fannie Mae-conforming mortgage, fifteen or thirty years. The down payment comes from a second, separate loan backed by the buyer’s Bitcoin or USDC. The crypto is held in custody while the loan is outstanding, and the buyer still owns it. According to the companies, price drops alone won’t trigger margin calls or liquidation. The risk comes if the borrower falls seriously behind on payments. Reported rates ran about half a point to a point and a half above a standard thirty-year mortgage, depending on the borrower.

That’s still leverage. It’s two loans, not one. Miss enough payments and you can lose both the house and the Bitcoin. Nobody should walk into it lightly.

But Mama Lou got it immediately when Marcus explained it.

“So the bank’s holding the Bitcoin like a pawn shop holds a ring.”

“Kind of, yeah.”

“And you get it back when you pay.”

“Yes, ma’am.”

“Hm,” she said. “My daddy would have liked to own something a bank wanted to hold.”

*  *  *

At Block Wall Street, we think the Bitcoin mortgage is one of the most important developments since the spot Bitcoin ETFs launched. This is our view, and here’s our reasoning.

ETFs added demand. They made it easy for anyone with a brokerage account to buy Bitcoin. But Bitcoin pledged against a thirty-year mortgage does something different. It removes supply. It gets locked away, often for years, and can’t be sold during that time. Only about 450 new bitcoin are created each day through mining. If even a modest share of homebuyers start locking Bitcoin into long-term collateral, the amount pulled off the market could become meaningful compared with new supply.

There’s a bigger signal, too. When the largest mortgage institution in the country accepts Bitcoin as collateral, the system is treating Bitcoin as wealth, not just speculation. Bitcoin stops competing only with gold and starts competing inside the housing market, which is measured in the trillions.

None of this is guaranteed. It’s a thesis. But it points to something we believe deeply: Bitcoin is becoming infrastructure, not just a trade.

Price moves every day, and most of that is noise. The signal is adoption. Is Bitcoin being built into lending? Into mortgages? Into retirement accounts? Are more people holding it for the long run? When those answers keep moving in the same direction year after year, the weekly price chart matters a lot less.

*  *  *

Before you borrow a dollar against anything, a few rules that Marcus learned, some of them the hard way. Keep your LTV low; many careful borrowers stay at or under 30%. Know your exact liquidation price, and write it down. Keep extra cash or collateral ready to add if the market crashes. Borrow for needs and productive uses, not impulse buys. Find out who holds your collateral and what happens to it if the lender goes under. Remember that interest keeps adding up, so the loan has to be paid. And talk to a tax professional, because borrowing generally isn’t taxable, but swaps, sales, and liquidations usually are.

Our ancestors were the collateral. Now we can hold it. That’s worth doing carefully.

Back to contents

Chapter 16

Feeding the Machine

Marcus’s first loan against his Bitcoin was for $400. He used it to fix his car’s transmission.

It was a small thing. But when he told his grandmother, she put her coffee cup down.

“You mean you didn’t have to touch your savings?”

“No, ma’am. The savings is still there. Still growing. I just borrowed against it.”

“And who’d you borrow from?”

“A computer program.”

She shook her head. But she was smiling.

*  *  *

In the old system, a bank takes your deposits, lends them out, and keeps most of the profit. DeFi makes it possible to do a lot of that banking for yourself. At Block Wall Street we call it self-banking.

It works in layers. Your savings are held in assets you control. Those assets can earn yield. They can serve as collateral for credit. And that credit can be put to work in things that produce income. Stack those layers together and you’ve got a financial machine working for you.

The most widely used DeFi lending protocol is Aave. It started in 2017 under the name ETHLend and grew into one of the biggest lending markets in crypto, running across many blockchains. We like to call it the JP Morgan of DeFi. People who supply assets to Aave earn interest from borrowers. People who borrow post collateral and take loans against it. Smart contracts, not loan officers, enforce the rules.

Aave tracks each borrower’s safety with something called a health factor. You take the value of your collateral, multiply it by the liquidation threshold, and divide by what you owe. Using Marcus’s example from the last chapter, $10,000 of Bitcoin with a 78% threshold and $3,000 borrowed, that’s $10,000 times 0.78, divided by $3,000, which comes out to 2.6. Anything above 1 is safe. At 1 or below, liquidation can start. The higher the number, the more room you have.

*  *  *

We teach people to build the foundation of their machine primarily with Bitcoin and Ethereum. They’re the two largest and most established digital assets. Almost every lender accepts them as collateral. Their markets are deep enough to borrow against in size. And both have long histories of recovering from brutal drawdowns. Smaller coins can have a place, but they make weak collateral. Lenders let you borrow less against them, and they’re far more likely to collapse without warning.

Once the foundation is in place, the machine runs on a loop. You earn income from your job, your business, or side work. You deposit a regular piece of it into Bitcoin and Ethereum on a lending protocol. You borrow a small percentage against your growing collateral, for living needs or productive uses. You put some of what you borrowed to work in things that produce income. And you send that income back in as more collateral.

Every deposit makes the foundation stronger. Every cycle raises how much you can safely borrow while keeping your LTV low. We call it feeding the machine.

Money from outside the machine can speed it up: odd jobs, business profits, a bonus, a tax refund. Marcus started putting half of every overtime check in.

*  *  *

The first real milestone is simple to say and hard to reach. It’s the point where your monthly passive income is greater than your monthly living expenses. We call it getting over the hump.

Before the hump, you feed the machine with your labor. After the hump, the machine can start feeding you, and every extra dollar you earn goes toward building more long-term wealth.

For most people starting from zero, getting over the hump takes years, often a full market cycle or longer. Starting when the market is down can actually be an advantage, because every deposit buys more.

Marcus isn’t over the hump yet. He’ll tell you that himself. But he knows exactly how far away it is, and he knows it’s getting closer.

*  *  *

One of the ways to put borrowed money to work is by providing liquidity to a decentralized exchange.

A liquidity pool holds two assets, say ETH and BTC, side by side. When traders swap one for the other, each trade pays a small fee to the people who supplied the liquidity. Some platforms add extra reward tokens on top.

But there’s a catch called impermanent loss. When the prices of the two assets drift apart, the pool automatically rebalances, and you can end up with less value than if you’d just held the two assets on their own. There are ways to soften this. You can pair assets that tend to move together, like ETH and BTC. You can choose wider price ranges on platforms that let you set them, earning less per dollar but needing less babysitting. Or you can pair Bitcoin with tokenized gold, which you’ll read about in Chapter 18, to add diversification.

Here’s the rule that matters most. If you put borrowed money into a pool, the pool has to earn more than your loan costs, after impermanent loss. Otherwise the machine is running backwards.

Rewards from a pool can be claimed or compounded. Claiming means pulling them out, either to live on or to send back into your lending position as more collateral. Compounding means putting them back into the pool so future fees are earned on a bigger position. Claiming strengthens the foundation. Compounding grows the engine. Most people end up doing some of both.

*  *  *

Artificial intelligence is starting to plug into all of this. AI agents can already watch positions, rebalance pools, warn you when a health factor drops, and carry out strategies around the clock. Major platforms, including Robinhood, have announced agent-based trading features. Automation can make self-banking more disciplined. It can also lose money very fast if it’s following bad instructions. Understand a strategy completely before you hand it to software.

*  *  *

None of this is safe by default. Collateral can get liquidated in a crash. Smart contracts can have bugs or get hacked. Interest rates on DeFi loans can jump suddenly. Liquidity pools carry impermanent loss. Stablecoins can lose their peg. People send money to the wrong address or approve a malicious contract with one careless tap. And the taxes on swaps and rewards can get complicated fast.

Start small. Learn the tools with money you can afford to lose. Scale up only after you understand every moving part.

Marcus’s $400 transmission loan was paid back in two months. It wasn’t a big move. But it was the first time in his family’s history that someone borrowed against something they owned, instead of being what someone else owned.

Back to contents

Chapter 17

Spending Without Selling

By 2025, Tasha’s nail shop was doing well enough that she started buying a little Bitcoin every week. Then she ran into the problem everybody runs into.

“It’s great that it’s growing,” she told Marcus. “But I live in the real world. The light bill doesn’t take Bitcoin.”

Building digital wealth is only half the challenge. The other half is living your everyday life without selling the very assets you’re trying to grow. A new wave of financial products, often called crypto neobanks, is trying to solve exactly that.

*  *  *

A neobank is a financial service that lives mostly in an app instead of a branch. Crypto neobanks usually offer some mix of debit or credit cards that spend stablecoins or crypto, credit lines backed by crypto collateral, yield on deposits, and cash-back rewards, sometimes paid in crypto.

The big idea for wealth builders is to spend against your assets, not spend your assets.

*  *  *

These products sit along a spectrum, and where a product sits changes everything about it.

At one end are the fully regulated companies that verify your identity, a process called KYC, which stands for “Know Your Customer.” Strike offers loans and credit lines against Bitcoin. SALT Lending, founded in 2016, was one of the very first crypto-backed lenders, and it has let borrowers pick their own risk level, with LTV options like 30%, 50%, or 70%, and it issues margin calls before liquidating. Companies like these operate inside traditional rules, which usually means more consumer protection, less privacy, and more restrictions.

In the middle are mixed models like ether.fi, Avici, and card programs such as Zebec. They combine self-custody or DeFi features with regular card networks. Most still check your identity for the card itself, and every one of them relies on outside card issuers and payment processors.

At the other end are non-custodial products with little or no KYC. Surge, a Bitcoin-native credit line, is built so you keep control of your Bitcoin through on-chain scripts rather than handing it to a company. Peer-to-peer marketplaces like Peer let people trade between regular money and crypto using cryptographic proof of payment instead of a middleman. Less company custody means less risk that a company fails with your money. It also means much more responsibility falls on you.

There’s no perfect spot on the spectrum. Each point trades something for something else.

*  *  *

One of the most important things Tasha learned is that many of these products aren’t available everywhere in the United States. State money-transmitter and lending laws differ, and companies often leave certain states out entirely. The only way to know is to read the company’s own eligibility page and confirm your state is on it. Watch out for look-alike products with similar names, too. And check again later, because availability changes.

*  *  *

Then there’s the story of Wirecard.

In June 2020, Wirecard, a major German payments company, collapsed after admitting that about €1.9 billion it claimed to have probably didn’t exist. Wirecard wasn’t a crypto company. But one of its subsidiaries issued payment cards for a lot of financial apps, including several crypto card programs. When regulators froze that subsidiary, people who held those crypto cards suddenly couldn’t use them, even though the crypto companies themselves had done nothing wrong.

Every card sits on a chain of companies: the app you see, the company that issues the card, the bank behind it, and the processor that moves the payment. If any link breaks, your access can vanish overnight. That’s a different risk from custody. You can hold your own crypto perfectly and still lose the ability to spend it through a card, because of a company whose name you’ve never heard.

*  *  *

So before Tasha signs up for any crypto card or credit line, she asks five questions. Who holds my assets: me, the company, or a partner? Who actually issues the card, and which bank and processor are behind it? Is it legally offered in Illinois? If there’s a loan, when and how can my collateral be sold? And how long has this company been around, and how did it handle the last crash?

Marketing pages describe the benefits. Your job is to find the risks. In the digital age, the most valuable financial skill you can have is the habit of checking for yourself.

Chapter 18

Gold, Stocks, and Digital Dollars

Mama Lou owned exactly one piece of gold: a thin chain her mother gave her the day she left Mississippi. She wore it every day for sixty years.

“Gold don’t lie,” she liked to say. “Paper lies. Gold don’t.”

So when Marcus showed her that he could now own gold on his phone, a real ounce sitting in a real vault, divided into pieces as small as he wanted, she looked at the screen for a long time.

“And you can send it to somebody? Like a text?”

“Yes, ma’am.”

“Lord,” she said. “What a world.”

*  *  *

One of the biggest changes in finance since the first edition of this book is that traditional assets are moving onto blockchains. It’s called tokenization. A real-world asset, like gold, a stock, or a dollar, is represented by a digital token that can sit in a wallet, move across the world, and be used in DeFi.

For communities that were locked out of asset markets for generations, tokenization lowers the walls. It lets you own a fraction of something expensive. It lets you trade at any hour instead of only during business hours. Transfers settle in seconds or minutes. Anyone with a supported wallet can take part, subject to local laws. And tokens can be plugged into everything else in this book, used as collateral or placed in liquidity pools.

*  *  *

Gold has been money for thousands of years, and tokenization makes it easier to hold, divide, and use. Two of the most widely used gold tokens are PAX Gold, known as PAXG, issued by Paxos, and Tether Gold, known as XAUT. Each token represents one troy ounce of physical gold held in professional vaults.

Gold and Bitcoin often move differently, which is why pairing them can make sense in a portfolio or a liquidity pool. Gold tends to hold steady in some crises. Bitcoin brings growth potential. Together they balance each other.

But a gold token is only as good as the company behind it. Before you buy, know who holds the gold, where it’s vaulted, and how it’s audited. Mama Lou was right that gold doesn’t lie. People still can.

*  *  *

Stocks are going on-chain too. The movement started with tokenized Treasury and fund products from firms like Ondo Finance. In 2025, tokenized stocks arrived on networks like Solana, including a product called xStocks. That June, Robinhood launched tokenized U.S. stocks and ETFs for eligible customers in Europe.

Then, on July 1, 2026, Robinhood launched the public version of its own blockchain, Robinhood Chain, built with Ethereum Layer 2 technology from Arbitrum and designed specifically for tokenized real-world assets. With it came Robinhood’s Stock Tokens, which trade around the clock and can be used in lending and liquidity pools.

Here’s what American readers need to know. According to Robinhood’s own disclosures, its Stock Tokens are tokenized debt securities that give economic exposure to a stock without giving you ownership rights in the actual shares, and they are not available to people in the United States. Many other tokenized stock products have similar limits. Always check whether you’re eligible before you try to buy anything.

*  *  *

The traditional U.S. stock market holds its regular trading session for six and a half hours a day, five days a week. That’s less than a fifth of the hours in a week. Tokenized markets can trade twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week. News that breaks on a Saturday can move tokenized prices long before Wall Street reopens on Monday.

For liquidity providers, that means fees can be earned during hours when traditional markets are dark. For everyone, it also means prices can swing hard at hours when there’s no traditional market to check them against.

And just like Bitcoin, tokenized stocks are starting to be accepted as collateral. Lending platforms on networks like Solana, including Kamino, have added tokenized stocks as collateral. The “don’t sell, collateralize” idea from Chapter 15 now reaches into stock portfolios.

*  *  *

Remember Deandra sending USDC to Kofi in Accra? That was a stablecoin, a token built to hold a steady value, usually one U.S. dollar. USDC, issued by a company called Circle, is one of the most widely used.

In July 2025, the United States passed the GENIUS Act, the first federal law setting up rules for payment stablecoins, including requirements for the reserves backing them and the disclosures issuers have to make.

Stablecoins have become the cash of DeFi. They’re what most people borrow when they take a collateralized loan. They move money across borders quickly and cheaply. And they’re the currency many tokenized assets settle in. There are even blockchains being built specifically for stablecoin payments, including Circle’s own network, Arc. For families sending money home across the diaspora, this could make remittances faster and cheaper than any wire service.

*  *  *

Tokenized assets carry their own risks. The company behind a token can fail or mishandle the reserves. A token might give you economic exposure without legal ownership. Rules differ from country to country and change constantly. A stablecoin can lose its dollar value, briefly or for good. And some tokens trade in thin markets, especially late at night and on weekends, where prices can jump around.

The rule is the same one Tasha uses for her credit cards: know exactly what a token represents, and know exactly who stands behind it.
