Chapter 19

What We Hold Together

After Sister Maxine’s burial society folded, Mama Lou never joined another one.

“I got burned once,” she said. “Once is enough.”

Marcus understood that. But he also understood what the family had lost when the society died. Not just the money. The safety of knowing forty people had your back.

So in 2025, Marcus, Deandra, Jaylen, Tasha, and a handful of friends from Block Wall Street classes started talking about building something together. They wanted to pool like the old societies did. They just didn’t want it to break the way the old societies did.

They started with the difference between two words people usually treat as the same.

*  *  *

A community Bitcoin reserve is long-term savings. Its job is to make the group stronger over decades. It’s rarely, if ever, spent. Think of it like a country’s gold reserve: its value comes from being there.

A community treasury is an operating fund. Its job is to be used: to fund programs, back local businesses, pay for education, and respond when members are in need.

The two work best together. The reserve grows quietly over the long haul. When the group needs money, it can borrow against the reserve instead of selling it, the same “don’t sell, collateralize” principle from Chapter 15, now working for a whole community. The treasury puts that money to work. And whatever the treasury’s work earns can flow back into the reserve.

*  *  *

The group spent more time on rules than on anything else, because rules are what Sister Maxine’s society didn’t have.

They set up a multi-signature wallet, three-of-five, which means any three of five keyholders have to approve before a single satoshi can move. No one person can take the money, and no one person’s illness or absence can lock it up. They wrote a policy spelling out what the reserve and treasury can and can’t be used for. They agreed to report balances openly, which is easy when anyone can check a blockchain. They made a plan for replacing keyholders. And they talked to a lawyer about forming a legal entity to hold the assets and sign agreements, because a group of friends with a wallet isn’t a legal organization.

The Freedman’s Savings Bank failed because depositors had no oversight. The burial society failed because everything depended on one person. This time, the oversight belongs to the members, and the system doesn’t depend on anyone’s health.

*  *  *

In their research, the group kept running into something called a Private Membership Association, or PMA. Online, PMAs are often sold as a way to operate outside regulation or taxes.

Be careful here. Courts have generally not accepted PMA status as a shield from licensing laws, securities laws, or tax laws. Calling your group an association doesn’t change what the law thinks lending money, selling investments, or practicing medicine is. Legitimate membership organizations still follow the law. An association can be a useful way to organize people around shared rules and purpose. It is not a loophole. Anyone considering one should talk to an attorney first.

*  *  *

One membership organization the group studied closely was the United Precious Metals Association, or UPMA. It’s a nonprofit founded in 2011 in Utah, a state that recognizes gold and silver coins as legal tender. UPMA offers members accounts denominated in gold and silver. Members can hold vaulted metal in their accounts, spend it with a payment card, borrow against it through a gold-backed line of credit, lease it out to earn a return paid in metal, and use the Goldback, a small spendable note made with real gold.

Mama Lou found UPMA fascinating. “So you can spend gold, and borrow on gold, and never sell the gold.”

“That’s the idea.”

“That’s the same thing you told me about the Bitcoin.”

She was right. UPMA brings together several ideas from this book: holding hard assets, borrowing against them instead of selling, and using an association and trust structure to organize ownership. As with any financial organization, anyone thinking about joining should study its terms, fees, custody arrangements, and legal structure carefully.

*  *  *

Then came the hardest conversation, the one about dying.

Wealth that can’t be passed down isn’t generational wealth. For Mama Lou’s generation, inheritance meant a house and maybe a coffee can. For Marcus’s generation, it might mean a hardware wallet in a drawer that nobody knows how to open.

That’s where trusts come in. A trust is a legal arrangement where a trustee holds assets for the benefit of beneficiaries, following written instructions. A common type is the revocable living trust. You can usually serve as your own trustee while you’re alive. You can change it or cancel it any time. When you die, a successor trustee you’ve chosen distributes your assets the way you said. And assets in the trust can often skip the delays and costs of probate court.

For digital assets, this matters even more than usual. A seed phrase with no instructions can mean money lost forever. Heirs may not even know the assets exist. And without a plan, state default rules decide who inherits, not you.

One of the most overlooked steps is also the simplest: naming beneficiaries. A trust or account without clearly named beneficiaries can pass assets in ways the owner never intended.

Marcus now keeps an updated list of what he owns and where it is. He’s named beneficiaries on every account. He has a plan for how his family could access his self-custodied Bitcoin without anyone seeing his seed phrase while he’s alive. He’s looked into multi-signature setups and inheritance services built for crypto. He plans to review it all after every big life change. And he’s working with an estate attorney who understands digital assets.

Mama Lou, for her part, finally put her house in a trust. She was eighty-four.

“I should have done this forty years ago,” she said.

“You’re doing it now,” Marcus said.

Chapter 20

The Keys

Jaylen called Marcus late on the night of July 30, 2026.

“You got a Coldcard?”

“No. Why?”

“Somebody’s draining them. Hundreds of wallets. Right now.”

*  *  *

Before we get to that night, let’s talk about the keys.

When your crypto sits on an exchange or in an app, the company controls the private keys, the secret codes that authorize spending. What you actually hold is an IOU. When exchanges collapse, customers can lose everything. Mt. Gox in 2014 and FTX in 2022 cost people billions of dollars.

Self-custody means you hold your own keys. No company can freeze your money, lend it out, or lose it. But self-custody also means no customer service line, no password reset, and nobody to call if you make a mistake.

Most wallets generate a seed phrase, usually twelve or twenty-four words, that can recreate every key in the wallet. Whoever has those words has the money. Never type your seed phrase into a website, an app, or a message. Never take a picture of it or put it in cloud storage or email. Store it offline, somewhere secure, ideally with a durable backup. And know this: no legitimate company or support agent will ever ask you for it.

*  *  *

A seed phrase is only secure if it was created from true randomness. The technical word is entropy.

A standard twelve-word seed phrase is designed to carry 128 bits of entropy. That’s so many possible combinations that no computer on earth could ever guess yours. But if the randomness is flawed, the number of possibilities can shrink dramatically, until a determined attacker can simply search through them.

That’s what happened the night Jaylen called.

*  *  *

In late July 2026, Coinkite, the company that makes the Coldcard hardware wallet, put out a security advisory. Seeds created on certain devices and firmware versions might have been generated with far less randomness than they were supposed to have.

According to public reporting, a firmware change made back in March 2021 caused affected devices to rely on a weak software random number generator instead of the hardware source they were designed to use. Researchers estimated that affected Mk3 seeds carried roughly 40 bits of entropy, and some newer models roughly 72 bits, instead of 128. On July 30 and 31, an attacker swept roughly 594 BTC, worth about $38 million, out of around 500 single-signature wallets in less than half an hour. Researchers later reported more waves and higher totals.

The part that hit hardest was who the victims were. Many had never shared their seed phrase. Never clicked a phishing link. Never plugged their device into the internet. They had done everything they were told to do. Their seeds were weak from the day they were created.

*  *  *

Marcus didn’t lose anything that night. But he didn’t sleep much either, and in the weeks after, he rebuilt his whole security setup. Here’s what that night taught him, and what it should teach all of us.

No tool is perfect. Even respected security products can carry hidden flaws for years. So keep your firmware updated and pay attention to official security notices from whoever makes your wallet. When your device lets you, add your own randomness when you create a seed, for example by rolling dice. Use a passphrase, an extra secret word that creates a completely separate wallet on top of your seed. For bigger holdings, think seriously about multi-signature. The wallets drained that night were reported to be single-signature, and a multi-signature wallet built with devices from different manufacturers doesn’t fail just because one manufacturer made a mistake.

And never, ever type your seed phrase into a “vulnerability checker.” Within days of the Coldcard news, scammers were putting up websites offering to check whether your wallet was affected. Every security scare brings them out.

*  *  *

Different amounts deserve different protection. Money you spend day to day can live in a reputable mobile wallet. Real savings belong on a hardware wallet with a passphrase and secure backups. Long-term or large holdings are best in multi-signature custody spread across several devices and locations. And community money, like the reserve Marcus and his friends built, should always be multi-signature with several independent keyholders and a written policy.

The everyday habits matter just as much. Use a password manager and a different password for everything. Use app-based or hardware two-factor authentication, not text messages. Check every address twice before you send. Revoke smart contract approvals you’re not using. Be suspicious of urgency, giveaways, and anyone offering to “help” recover your money. And keep your holdings to yourself. Talking publicly about your wealth makes you a target.

*  *  *

Greenwood’s wealth was burned in a night. The Freedman’s Bank lost its depositors’ savings through someone else’s mismanagement. Mama Lou lost her burial dues when the book stopped being kept.

Ownership without protection is temporary. That was true in 1921, and it’s true now. The threats look different, but the principle hasn’t changed. Protecting what you own is every bit as important as building it.

Back to contents

Epilogue

The Coffee Can, Again

Mama Lou turned eighty-five in the spring of 2026. The family threw her a party in the backyard of the brick house on the South Side, the one now held in a trust with her grandchildren named as beneficiaries.

After the cake, she asked Marcus to go get something from the pantry.

It was the coffee can. The same red Maxwell House can, the lid still not sitting quite flat.

She took the money out, counted it right there at the picnic table, and handed it to him.

“Put it in the machine,” she said.

“Mama Lou, you don’t have to…”

“Boy, I know I don’t have to. I’m telling you to.” She tapped the table. “My daddy never owned a thing. I owned this house and this can. You’re gonna own more than that. And your children are gonna own more than you. That’s how it’s supposed to go.”

*  *  *

Everything in this book comes back to a few lessons. They aren’t really about crypto. They’re about how wealth gets built, in any era.

Own things. Consuming makes other people rich. Owning is what builds wealth for you. Income pays for today. Assets pay for generations.

Understand the technology. The next era of economic power is being built on digital infrastructure. The people who understand it, and especially the people who build it, will shape who benefits. Learning is the cheapest asset you’ll ever buy.

Build together. Individuals can build wealth. Organized communities build power. Our ancestors knew this in the Free African Society, in Greenwood, in Bronzeville, and in every burial society in every church basement. What’s new is that we finally have tools to make shared money transparent, protected, and independent of any one person.

Don’t sell your future. Hold the assets that grow. Borrow against them carefully instead of giving them up. Our ancestors were the collateral. We get to hold it.

Protect what you build. Wealth that can be burned, frozen, stolen, or lost to a weak seed phrase isn’t secure. Custody, security, trusts, and named beneficiaries are what turn wealth into generational wealth.

Watch the signal, not the noise. Prices will crash again. Hype will come and go. Some projects will fail and some people will get hurt. Pay attention to adoption, to what’s actually being built, and stay patient through the cycles that every major technology has gone through.

*  *  *

No single technology is going to undo four hundred years of history. Bitcoin won’t do it. DeFi won’t do it. Tokenization won’t do it. What these tools can do is give us better material to build with than any generation before us had. Wealth that can’t be burned. Ledgers that can’t be cooked. Shared funds that don’t fall apart when one person gets sick. A path to borrow against what we own instead of being what someone else owns.

Understanding these tools is the first step. What we choose to build with them is up to us.

Marcus still has the coffee can. It’s empty now, sitting on a shelf in his apartment. He keeps it there on purpose.

It reminds him where we started.

And how far we still have to go.
